title: Compute as Teacher: Turning Inference Compute Into Reference-Free Supervision
claim: A closed loop turns the policy's own parallel samples into a pseudo-reference, then into rewards that improve that policy.
layout: 2 rows, snake-shaped loop; arrows run left-to-right, then right-to-left; dashed feedback arrow
description: A two-row flow diagram. The top row runs left to right through rounded boxes: prompt q, policy π_t, rollouts o1…oG, a dashed grey box labelled Reference Estimation, and a green box for the pseudo-reference s. A thick arrow goes down from s to the bottom row. The bottom row runs right to left: a dashed grey Reward Derivation box, an orange box of rewards R1…RG, an RL box, and the updated policy π_{t+1}. A dashed grey feedback arrow loops from π_{t+1} and RL back up to π_t. Small grey captions sit above and below the boxes. They name the variants: synthesis / majority / BoN under Reference Estimation, and rubrics / answer match under Reward Derivation. A cartoon wizard cat sits in the middle as a mascot. Colour is limited to green and orange, which pick out the pseudo-reference and the rewards. The eye goes first to the top-left prompt box and follows the arrows.
caption: \methodabb framework. The policy $\pi_t$ generates $G$ rollouts for prompt $q$. Reference estimation (synthesis, majority vote, or best-of-N) aggregates them into pseudo-reference $s$. Reward derivation scores each rollout against $s$: answer matching for verifiable domains, self-proposed rubrics for non-verifiable. Rewards drive RL, updating the policy.
abstract: Where do learning signals come from when there is no ground truth in post-training? We show that inference compute itself can serve as supervision. By generating parallel rollouts and converting them into reference estimates, models can learn without human labels-critically, even in non-verifiable domains like healthcare guidance where no programmatic checker exists. We call this framework Compute as Teacher (CaT) and it turns inference-time compute from parallel rollouts into supervision for RL training. The framework has two components: (1) reference estimation which aggregates rollouts into a pseudo-reference answer, and (2) reward derivation which converts that pseudo-reference into RL rewards. For (1), we explore a simple method we call synthesis, but the framework admits any aggregator. For (2), we introduce self-proposed rubrics for non-verifiable domains. These are binary, auditable criteria generated from the pseudo-reference and scored by an LLM judge. On HealthBench, models trained with CaT match or exceed inference-time aggregation quality while using 9x less test-time compute. Here, CaT also competes with learning from expert physician annotations, yielding up to +30% relative improvement over the initial policy. The framework extends naturally to verifiable rewards, matching the best existing baselines on MATH-500 in test-time RL and demonstrating 'drop-in' versatility across both types of domains.
